quote: I just got a Tesla. And as I was thinking about it, I was like, hey. What if I just charge this off of the sun?
stewart_read: The customer just bought an EV and self-generated the solar idea from wanting to charge it — this is a higher-load, highly qualified enthusiasm signal, plus a natural bridge to mention Ion carries the Tesla Powerwall for backup.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to reflect this back explicitly ('so this would let you basically drive on sunlight') to build anchor-worthy curiosity rather than only noting it for the design team.

quote: We've got, you know, a van. I mean, it's, like, six or 7,000 square feet. So... I think we use about 4,000 kilowatt hours a month.
stewart_read: Customer hands over a large usage figure unprompted alongside home size context — a strong anchor — and the rep files it ('trying to get a feel for what something might look like') without reflecting it back as a hook.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep may be deliberately deferring detailed math to the closer to avoid setter scope creep, which is schema-correct, but reflecting the number back is different from explaining savings and would not have been scope creep.
coaching_implication: Show the rep the difference between explaining numbers (scope creep) and simply echoing the customer's own number back for curiosity ('4,000 kWh a month, that's a big number — the design team's going to have fun with this one').

stewart_read: A high, specific bill figure is captured cleanly, but the rep's very next line moves straight to averaging kWh rather than using the number emotionally.
coaching_implication: This is the clearest flip opportunity on the call — coach the rep to acknowledge the size of the number out loud before moving to the next verify item.

quote: Okay. Gotcha. Sounds good. And let's see. 4,000 is kind of average throughout the year per kilowatts per month?
stewart_read: Immediately after hearing a $500-600 bill, the rep pivots to a logistics question instead of flipping the bill into emotional leverage against the utility.
alternative_hypothesis: The call is short and the rep may be pacing toward booking quickly given the customer is already warm, so skipping the flip could be a deliberate low-friction strategy for an easy close — but the schema treats bill capture without flip as a standing gap regardless of ease.
coaching_implication: Even on easy, pre-sold leads, the bill flip strengthens the customer's own reason to sit through the closer's proposal instead of shopping further.

quote: Well yeah. And then I'll make a note here, that you got a Tesla. So are you planning on charging from home then?
stewart_read: Rep does circle back to the Tesla detail here, which is a partial, appropriate use of the interest reason — noted for the design team rather than pitched as a feature, consistent with setter scope discipline.
alternative_hypothesis: This could be read as underuse of the EV signal since it stops at logistics ('charging from home') rather than reinforcing it as the customer's stated reason for calling at all.
coaching_implication: Good instinct to log the EV-charging detail for the design team; next step is to also verbally tie it back to the customer's own opening motivation before moving to booking.

quote: Yeah. My wife. It's actually in her name, I think, officially.
stewart_read: Customer discloses the home is titled in his wife's name — a co-owner fact adjacent to (but not identical to) the spouse-decision-maker trigger — and the rep replies with a filler acknowledgment and moves straight to utility questions without asking whether she should join the appointment.
alternative_hypothesis: Because this surfaced as a title-ownership fact rather than an explicit 'I need to talk to my spouse' statement, the rep may not have registered it as the spouse-inclusion protocol trigger at all, which is a related but distinct gap from a protocol violation.
coaching_implication: Coach the rep to treat any co-title disclosure as a cue to ask who should be on the appointment, even when it isn't phrased as a decision-deferral objection.

quote: Yeah. It looks like the soonest we could do would probably be looks like they do actually have someone pretty close to your area tomorrow.
stewart_read: The scheduling process takes several rounds of back-and-forth (tomorrow declined, week-of-third proposed, Monday declined, Wednesday declined, finally Friday) before landing on a date, showing some booking fragility even though it resolves.
alternative_hypothesis: This could read as poor pre-qualification of availability, but the transcript shows normal customer schedule constraints rather than rep-caused confusion — the rep stayed patient and flexible through each pivot.
coaching_implication: No correction needed on rep behavior here; flag for the manager only as a reminder that reconfirmation before Friday the 7th is now load-bearing given how many times the date moved.

quote: I'll get that on my calendar here, and I'll send you a text with the day and time.
stewart_read: The rep confirms date/time, promises a text, and mentions a Thursday check-in call, but never runs the explicit 'is that fair?' handshake or the no-driving/computer-ready instruction before signing off.
alternative_hypothesis: The rep's Thursday-reconfirmation promise partially substitutes for the handshake by building in a second touchpoint, softening the risk.
coaching_implication: Add the one-hour-block and no-driving/computer-ready language plus an explicit fairness check before ending calls — cheap insurance against no-shows on a two-week-out appointment.
